title: Phase diagram of a double-occupancy cell model of a fluid with Curie-Weiss interaction
authors: R. V. Romanik, O. A. Dobush, M. P. Kozlovskii, I. V. Pylyuk, M. A. Shpot
abstract: A double-occupancy cell model of a fluid with Curie-Weiss interaction is studied. First, we show that the model is isomorphic to the Blume-Capel model on a complete graph through a simple transformation from spin to occupancy variables. We then investigate its phase behavior within the grand-canonical ensemble using a combination of analytical and numerical methods. Despite its simplicity, the model exhibits a remarkably rich thermodynamic behavior depending on the ratio between the local repulsive and global attractive interactions. We identify regimes characterized by a single critical point, two distinct critical points, tricritical behavior, and triple-point formation. For sufficiently strong repulsion, the system possesses three fluid phases of different densities, leading to both gas-liquid and liquid-liquid coexistence. The locations of the critical, tricritical, and triple points are determined, and the corresponding phase diagrams are constructed. These results demonstrate that the competition between double-occupancy repulsion and long-range attraction is sufficient to generate complex phase behavior in a minimal multiple-occupancy lattice-gas model.
summary: This theoretical study investigates a double-occupancy cell fluid model interacting via Curie-Weiss forces. By analyzing its grand canonical partition function, the authors map out a complex phase diagram showing multiple coexistence regimes. The results demonstrate how simple competition between local repulsion and long-range attraction can generate rich physics, including liquid-liquid transitions.
main_problem: The study focuses on determining the complex phase diagram of a fluid modeled by a double-occupancy cell model interacting via Curie-Weiss type long-range forces.
main_result: The competition between local repulsion and global attraction generates rich thermodynamic behavior, including regimes with single or two critical points, tricritical points, and triple points, leading to gas-liquid and liquid-liquid coexistence.
method: The analysis employs the grand canonical ensemble formalism, utilizing analytical techniques combined with numerical methods, notably applying Laplace's method to evaluate integrals in the thermodynamic limit.
model_or_system: The system is a double-occupancy cell fluid model where each site can hold up to two particles. This model is shown to be isomorphic to the Blume-Capel model on a complete graph.
key_observables: Phase diagram structure, critical points $(T^*_c; ho^*_c)$, tricritical points, triple points, and the pair distribution function $g(2)$.
important_parameters: The phase behavior is critically dependent on the ratio $a = \Delta/J$, which controls the balance between local repulsion ($\Delta$) and global attraction ($J$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on approximations in the thermodynamic limit ($N 	o \infty$) and uses mean-field descriptions, meaning it neglects local structural ordering effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagram showing lines of critical points for varying $a$, meeting at a tricritical point. Other figures show coexistence lines and spatial dependencies of pair distribution functions across different phases (I, II, III).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model's isomorphism to the Blume-Capel model. It then derives the partition function in the grand canonical ensemble, evaluates it using Laplace's method, and finally maps out the phase diagram by analyzing the conditions for critical points and coexistence lines as a function of the interaction ratio $a$.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the mapping to the Blume-Capel model connects this work to quantum spin systems, making it relevant for understanding phase transitions in lattice models that share mathematical structure with quantum Hamiltonians.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Phase diagram of the double-occupancy cell model in the case of distinguishable particles. Blue curve: the line of critical points at a < atc. Red curves: the lines of critical points at a > atc. Black curve: the line of triple points in the interval atc < a < 0.5. All the lines meet at the tricritical point with a = atc = 1

Fig. 2: The T ∗−ρ∗phase diagrams of the double-occupancy cell model in the case of distinguishable particles at different values of a = ∆/J. Solid curves are the coexistence lines. (a): The coexistence line between phases I and III ends at the critical point. (b) and (c): Coexistence lines between phases I — II and II — III are present in the temperature interval T ∗ tr ≤T ∗≤T ∗ c , each ending at its own critical point. For T ∗≤T ∗ tr, phases I and III coexist. T ∗ tr is the temperature of the triple point. (d): Coexistence lines between phases I — II and II — III are present for 0 ≤T ∗≤T ∗ c , each ending at its own critical point.

Fig. 3: The phase diagram in the (T ∗, ρ∗, a)-space for the case of distinguishable particles. The figure combines representations of Figs. 1 and 2 in one view. Green dashed curves: the coexistence lines at a = 0.3, a = 0.375, a = 0.45, and a = 0.6. Blue and red curves are the critical-point lines. Black curve is the triple-point line.

Fig. 4: Pair distribution function g(2)(r1, r2) as a function of separation r = |r1 −r2|. The quantity r∗denotes distance from the point with coordinate r1 to the boundary of the cubic cell containing r1, in the direction of r2. The results are presented for the system of distinguishable particles, at a = 0.5. Phase I: T ∗= 0.25, ρ∗= 0.1; Phase II: T ∗= 0.2, ρ∗= 0.5; Phase III: T ∗ c = 0.25, ρ∗= 1.9; Supercritical: T ∗= 0.5, ρ∗= 0.5. At r > r∗, g(2) = 1.
